Female Murray River turtles attain sexual maturity at a plastron length of approximately 18.7 centimeters [Lp = approximately 18.7 centimeters], whereas males reach puberty at a significantly smaller size of about 14.7 centimeters [Lp = about 14.7 centimeters]. These impressive adult dimensions underscore the considerable growth trajectory from the 2.7-centimeter hatchling, a process that spans several years and demands consistent access to high-quality foraging grounds within the riverine habitat.

The maximum reproductive rate of Emydura macquarii, observed under favorable captive conditions at a stable temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], corresponds to approximately 36 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 36 eggs per year]. The timing of nesting is closely tied to the seasonal flooding regime of the Murray-Darling system, as high water levels facilitate access to suitable nesting sites and may influence the thermal environment experienced by developing embryos. Females do not breed every year in wild populations, as the energetic cost of egg production and the risk of nest predation can lead to intermittent reproductive effort. The species' relatively high fecundity is thought to offset high mortality rates during the early life stages, particularly among hatchlings and juveniles.

Longevity records for Emydura macquarii indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 20.9 years [am = approximately 20.9 years] under the thermal conditions typical of the species' natural range, maintained at 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. The extended reproductive window afforded by such longevity allows females to compensate for years of low recruitment through repeated nesting attempts over several decades. Population viability analyses suggest that the combination of a lifespan of approximately two decades, a delay of roughly a decade to female puberty, and a maximum annual fecundity of approximately three dozen eggs is sufficient to sustain populations under moderate levels of subadult mortality. The species' ability to persist in variable riverine environments is further enhanced by its omnivorous diet, which includes aquatic invertebrates, algae, and carrion, providing dietary flexibility when preferred prey items are scarce. Conservation efforts for this species must therefore consider the preservation of both nesting habitat and long-term water flow regimes that support the extended maturation and reproductive schedules characteristic of this austral chelid.
